Trump is heading to China with Iran and nuclear arms on the agenda for possible talks with Xi and Putin, and he says he would gladly bring Jensen Huang along, a show of support that could become a test of Huang’s political standing. US President Donald Trump said he expects to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at next week’s APEC summit in China. He also said he would be willing to take Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang on the trip, despite the controversy over Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said a meeting with Xi and Putin “will be interesting” and would cover a lot of ground, including denuclearisation and ending the war in Iran, Reuters reported. Such a meeting would bring the leaders of the US, China and Russia together as the Iran conflict grinds through its eighth month. On Huang, Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia chief about the allegations but described him as a fine and honourable person who had done an amazing job for the United States. He added that Huang probably had an explanation and that it should be heard, while acknowledging that “you never know what is going on.” Asked whether Huang would join him in Asia, Trump said he did not know but would certainly take him. Trump’s remarks came on the same day that Huang admitted to a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom US officials reportedly believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, and that Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation. The board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and Huang remains chief executive. Whether Huang travels to China alongside the president will be closely watched. His presence would signal that the White House still sees him as a key voice on AI and chip policy. His absence would suggest the affair has begun to cost him political access at a sensitive moment for US export controls. In a lighter moment, Trump said he had only been kidding about naming Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive Dana White as White House press secretary. He said White loved the idea and that the two would speak on Monday about other matters. For markets, the APEC summit now looms as a significant event, with any progress on Iran carrying implications for oil and any signal on chips bearing directly on Nvidia. Stablecoin liquidity is the pressure point to watch, because Tether sits at the centre of crypto trading. A memecoin issuer has no such role. The WLFI token and the USD1 stablecoin face the most direct reputational risk from the probe. Bitcoin and ether face only indirect, sentiment-driven exposure. Blumenthal has spent most of a year writing letters to crypto firms; from January his requests come with the power to compel answers. US Senator Richard Blumenthal has given Binance, Tether and two crypto businesses tied to President Donald Trump until January 4, 2027, to hand over outstanding records, and the date matters more than the demand. It falls one day after the new Congress convenes, when Blumenthal is expected to take the chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations following the Democrats’ sweep of both chambers in the November 3 midterms. The letters, announced on November 5, went to Binance, Tether, World Liberty Financial and Fight Fight Fight LLC, the company behind the TRUMP memecoin. World Liberty and Fight Fight Fight were asked to begin producing documents by November 30. Blumenthal warned the subcommittee would look at other ways to secure compliance if the records were not delivered by the January deadline, and coverage of the Democratic sweep has read that as a signal subpoenas could follow. CNN reported that the same round of letters also went to Trump administration officials and several large corporate donors. None of the underlying lines of inquiry is new. Blumenthal opened his investigation into World Liberty Financial and the TRUMP coin in May 2025. In February he pressed Binance over a reported $1.7 billion in Iran-linked transfers, which the exchange disputed, saying its sanctions-related exposure had fallen sharply since early 2024. In October he wrote to Tether over reported payments to a consulting firm co-founded by former White House crypto adviser Bo Hines, which Tether has said involved no wrongdoing, and to Cantor Fitzgerald over its ties to the stablecoin issuer. What has changed is leverage. As the minority’s ranking member, Blumenthal could only ask for voluntary cooperation, and recipients are not obliged to respond until the new Congress is seated. From January, the requests come from a subcommittee chair with the tools to compel documents. For Bitcoin and ether, the direct price impact looks limited for now. The market has already absorbed the larger political shock: Bitcoin briefly fell below $76,000 as results came in on November 4 before recovering, while ether dropped to a two-month low in the same move, according to market reports. The letters target named companies, not the assets themselves. A longer wait for clear US rules would likely weigh on sentiment more than any single letter. Ether’s sharper election-week drop suggests it has been the more sensitive of the two to US policy risk, though that is an observation from one move rather than a fixed relationship. body: A hot PPI and a soft CPI is a poor mix for China’s growth outlook. It points to margin compression for manufacturers and weak domestic demand, which weighs on sentiment toward Chinese equities and keeps expectations of policy support alive. For the yuan, softer underlying inflation argues for easier policy at the margin, a mild negative. For the Australian dollar and commodity currencies, the read is mixed: firm producer prices reflect cost pressure rather than a demand-led recovery in China’s appetite for raw materials. For oil, the PPI surge mainly shows the energy shock feeding through, not new demand strength. China’s factories are facing their fastest price rises in years while consumer inflation slips further below 1%, a split that points to squeezed margins and fragile domestic demand rather than any healthy reflation. China’s factory-gate inflation accelerated more sharply than expected in October, while consumer price growth slowed below forecasts. The result widens the gap between surging producer costs and weak household demand. The producer price index rose 5.7% from a year earlier, well above expectations of around 5.3% and up from 5% in September, when it had already reached a four-year high. Consumer prices increased 0.7% year-on-year, slightly below the 0.8% forecast and down from 0.9% in September. They were flat on the month, in line with expectations, after a 0.2% gain in September. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, eased to 0.8% from 1%, also undershooting forecasts of 0.9%. The divergence between the two measures has now widened to around five percentage points. Producer prices are being driven higher by energy and other input costs, while consumer prices show little sign of following. That suggests manufacturers and retailers are absorbing much of the cost increase rather than passing it on, a reflection of soft domestic demand and limited pricing power. The core reading is the more telling figure for the health of the domestic economy. A slowdown in underlying inflation to below 1% points to subdued demand for services and non-essential goods, despite some support from spending around the National Day Golden Week holiday at the start of October. For policymakers, the mix is awkward. Weak consumer and core inflation strengthens the case for further support for domestic demand. The jump in producer prices, though, limits room for aggressive easing and squeezes industrial profit margins at a time when firms are already facing higher energy costs linked to the war with Iran. The data come as Beijing is also moving to shore up confidence in its stock market, with a recent State Council meeting calling for stronger capital market stabilisation mechanisms. Attention now turns to October trade data due on Tuesday, which will show whether export strength can continue to offset sluggish domestic demand. body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar Iraq's campaign for a larger OPEC production allocation has taken a complicated turn after Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said the country is already producing more than 5 million barrels per day , more than half a million barrels above its current OPEC+ requirement. Khudair’s statement raises a basic question over Iraq’s current production as OPEC prepares to set production levels for 2027. Just six days earlier, Baghdad joined six other OPEC+ producers in agreeing to maintain current production requirements for December, leaving Iraq at 4.431 million bpd. Shortly after Khudair put Iraqi production above 5 million bpd, the Oil Ministry reaffirmed Iraq's commitment to the 4.431 million bpd ceiling, saying October production had increased but giving no figure. Baghdad has spent months trying to persuade OPEC to recognize substantially more Iraqi production capacity. Iraq is seeking a future baseline based on capacity of around 6 million bpd, while OPEC is independently assessing members' maximum sustainable production capacity as it prepares its 2027 production framework. Iraq reported production of 4.399 million bpd to OPEC in September, before the Oil Ministry reported a further increase in October without providing a figure. Khudair said Iraq remained compliant with OPEC because its exports were within what he described as the group’s “export ceiling.” But Iraq’s 4.431 million bpd OPEC+ requirement is a production target, not an export target. OPEC’s rules are explicit on this point. Compliance is assessed using crude oil production , based on estimates from independent secondary sources. As Bloomberg’s Javier Blas has explained , OPEC+ has occasionally allowed individual countries to make commitments based partly on exports, most notably Russia, creating an increasingly complicated collection of cuts and targets. But that is not how Iraq’s current 4.431 million bpd requirement is defined: it applies to crude production. For Iraq, exports and production can differ significantly. Crude produced in Iraq can be exported, domestically refined, directly consumed for power generation or moved into storage. Iraq’s OPEC+ requirement, however, is measured against crude production rather than the volume ultimately exported. Related: The Iran War Isn't Over, but Oil Traders Are Already Pricing In Peace That is why Khudair’s explanation does not resolve the problem created by his own production figure. Iraq could export less than 4.431 million bpd and still produce more than its OPEC+ requirement. And if Khudair’s figure of more than 5 million bpd refers to crude production as OPEC defines it, it would put Iraqi output at least 569,000 bpd above the nominal requirement. OPEC does not simply use Baghdad’s reported production number when assessing compliance. It uses estimates from independent secondary sources, and those estimates can differ substantially from Iraq’s own figures. Khudair’s statement therefore does not establish that OPEC itself will record Iraqi production above 5 million bpd. But his reference to exports does not explain how production above that level would comply with Iraq’s production requirement. The U.S.-Iran war has radically changed the relationship between production and exports across the Gulf. For months, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have been producing below their OPEC+ allowances as the closure of Hormuz and continuing shipping disruptions restricted Gulf exports. That raises an obvious question as to whether OPEC has quietly become more interested in how much oil its members can actually export than how much they produce. So far, there is no direct indication that it has. OPEC’s Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC) directly addressed the disruption to international maritime routes in October, but continued to assess members using crude oil production data and adherence to production adjustments. title: Goldman Sachs Cuts Gold Price Forecasts as Hawkish Federal Reserve Weighs on Demand - Yahoo Finance
body: Goldman Sachs has lowered its gold price forecasts for the end of 2026 and 2027, citing the Federal Reserve's increasingly hawkish monetary policy stance and its impact on investor demand. However, the investment bank maintained a positive longer-term outlook, supported by substantial central bank purchases. Strategists led by Lina Thomas reduced their end-2026 gold price target to $4,150 per ounce from $4,650. The forecast for the end of 2027 was lowered to $4,800 per ounce from $5,400. The revised projections assume that the Fed's tighter policy stance, including an anticipated interest rate increase in December, will limit demand for gold as protection against currency depreciation and broader economic policy risks. Goldman expects investor demand for gold as a hedge against monetary and fiscal uncertainty to return toward historical averages rather than revisit the elevated levels recorded earlier in 2026. The bank compared current market conditions with 2022, when strong central bank purchases supported gold prices but higher interest rates limited investment demand. Higher borrowing costs generally reduce the attractiveness of gold because the precious metal does not generate interest income. Goldman also expects demand for gold call options, which can reflect investor interest in protection against policy-related risks, to moderate. Despite reducing its near-term forecasts, Goldman continues to view central bank demand as a significant structural driver of gold prices. The bank expects central banks to purchase approximately 60 tonnes of gold per month throughout 2026 and 2027, substantially above the average of 17 tonnes recorded before 2022. Its latest estimate places current purchases at approximately 85 tonnes per month, based on a seasonally adjusted three-month average. "We retain our longer-term constructive view on structurally strong central bank demand – which drives most of the 15% price upside we forecast by end-2027," the strategists wrote. Goldman noted that emerging-market central banks, particularly China, continue to hold relatively low gold allocations compared with potential long-term reserve targets. Developed-market central banks have generally participated less in the recent purchasing trend, partly because they already maintain substantial historical gold reserves. "But the debate is increasingly shifting from whether to own gold to where to store it, pointing to broader concerns around reserve security and cross-country trust," the strategists added. Goldman expects gold prices to receive additional support when the Federal Reserve begins reducing interest rates. The bank's economists anticipate rate cuts beginning in late 2027 and continuing into early 2028, potentially easing pressure on gold and encouraging renewed private investment demand. For shorter-term investors, however, the outlook remains challenging. Goldman identified rising interest rates, uncertain energy prices and restrictive risk limits as potential obstacles for commodity trading advisers and macro hedge funds over the next three to six months. Higher oil prices could also trigger additional selling by systematic investment strategies. The bank warned that gold could face further downward pressure if the Fed raises rates again in March 2027, delays monetary easing or increases its projected terminal interest rate. Under that scenario, Goldman estimates gold could reach $4,660 per ounce by the end of 2027, below its revised base-case forecast of $4,800. Conversely, renewed concerns about government debt sustainability and fiscal policy could increase demand for gold as a hedge, potentially pushing prices above the bank's central forecast. Goldman suggested that longer-term investors seeking exposure to sustained central bank purchases or protection against economic policy risks may view the current correction as a potential entry opportunity.

title: Bank of England raises interest rates, signals further hikes - Big News Network.com
body: LONDON, U.K.: The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4 percent on November 5, its first increase in more than three years, warning that further tightening could be necessary as the US-Iran conflict continues to drive up energy costs and threaten Britain's inflation outlook. The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to increase its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point from 3.75 percent. The lone dissenter, Catherine Mann, supported a larger half-point increase to 4.25 percent. The decision comes as the bank forecasts inflation will reach approximately 5 percent by the middle of next year, more than twice its 2 percent target, creating further cost-of-living challenges for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government. "Today's increase shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase," Governor Andrew Bailey said. Although the bank has seen limited evidence of accelerating inflation outside sectors directly affected by higher energy costs, policymakers concluded that months of elevated prices had created sufficient future inflationary pressure to justify immediate action. Consumer price inflation reached 3.5 percent in September, raising concerns among some policymakers that inflation expectations could become harder to control. Mann, who had previously criticised the bank for being too slow to reassure markets about inflation, cited "non-linear inflation risks" and warned of a possible loss of confidence in the central bank. Financial markets had widely anticipated Thursday's increase and were pricing in three further quarter-point hikes during 2027, more than most economists expect. Bailey said the difference reflected financial markets accounting for the possibility of a sharper rise in energy prices, while economists generally based their forecasts on a more moderate tightening cycle. "Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates," he said in the policy minutes. Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli also indicated that another increase would probably be needed in the near term. External policymaker Megan Greene called for "further tightening", while Chief Economist Huw Pill referred to the need for "additional hikes". However, policymakers Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor said they would require stronger evidence of secondary inflationary effects before supporting additional increases. Alongside the rate decision, the Bank of England upgraded its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to 1.6 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, exceeding projections issued by the government's Office for Budget Responsibility last week. The bank attributed some of the stronger outlook to investment in artificial intelligence and a modest temporary boost from Finance Minister John Healey's annual budget. Under its central forecast, inflation is expected to peak at an average of 4.8 percent in the second quarter of 2027. In a more adverse scenario, with oil prices reaching approximately $130 a barrel instead of around $100, inflation could climb to 6.2 percent in the third quarter of 2027. The bank now expects inflation to return to its 2 percent target only in the third quarter of 2028, six months later than it projected in July. It also forecast that British households' income from work, after accounting for inflation and taxes, would decline both this year and next. The government's latest budget is expected to reduce inflation by 0.25 percentage points at its peak, although the bank warned that inflation could rise again when temporary cost-of-living support measures expire.

body: The European Central Bank voted to hold interest rates steady on Thursday, meeting market expectations, despite euro zone inflation rising to a three-year high. It keeps the central bank's key rate, the deposit facility, at 2.5% following a 25 basis point hike in September . In a statement, the institution's Governing Council said rising energy prices posed upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to growth, but that underlying inflation and wages were so far broadly stable. "At this point in time we are not seeing second round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections" released in September, ECB President Christine Lagarde told CNBC's Annette Weisbach during a press conference. Lagarde identified the main developments since the ECB's last meeting as higher energy costs across oil, petrol, fuel, gas and refining margins, and a sharp rise in long-term financing costs, with the average 10-year sovereign yield up by around 35 basis points. "If you combine these two factors — actually, the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate — but on the basis of the uncertainty that accumulates and that rises as well, on the basis of underlying inflation that has broadly remained unchanged, the Governing Council unanimously decided that we were well positioned enough at this stage to hold and that a measured approach at this point in time remained appropriate," Lagarde said. Money markets were pricing in around a 67% probability of a rate hike in December following the announcement, according to LSEG data. Headline inflation in the euro area hit 3.8% last month , the highest level since September 2023. Energy price inflation reached 18.8% amid continued turbulence in the Middle East. The resurgence in energy price pressures following the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February saw the ECB hike rates in June for the first time since 2023. The euro area economy continued to expand in the third quarter of the year, with a recovery in services since the start of the Middle East conflict, the Governing Council said in an explanation of its decision Thursday. Manufacturing, digital services and exports are being boosted by AI-related investments, while government spending on infrastructure and defense is supporting business activity. However, energy price pressures are likely to hit consumer confidence as higher financing costs weigh on growth. In her press conference, Lagarde said the ECB would continue monitoring rising French borrowing costs and increased fragmentation that has spooked some market watchers. Lagarde noted borrowing costs at the long end of the curve were rising significantly around the world, which she attributed to expectations for inflation and interest rates as well as "debt issuance by some of the hyperscalers," which she said were issuing more long-term bonds and driving up competition. "Predicting the path of ECB monetary policy is becoming more challenging," Deutsche Bank's chief European economist, Mark Wall, said in a note on Thursday. "One question is whether the two hikes already delivered and the tightening of financial conditions since September are enough to lean against the further increase in energy inflation risk? Probably not." Wall said the other main question was whether the looming departure of Lagarde as ECB president — a decision she announced earlier on Thursday — would impact decision-making next year. "We think the institution is bigger than the person, but there's uncertainty. We expect one more hike to 2.75% in December while Lagarde is still President, and that's probably the end of the hiking cycle." title: Third-quarter U.S. GDP increases a better-than-expected 3.4% as September inflation accelerates
summary: The personal consumption expenditures price index was projected to increase 0.5% in September for an annual rate of 3.7%, according to the Dow Jones consensus.
body: The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move. "The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday. However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do. A Labor Department report also released Thursday showed that layoffs remain low. Initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the estimate for 200,000 and near levels last seen in the late 1960s. Stock market future s were negative following the releases while Treasury yields also fell. "Net, net, economic growth is powering ahead despite the uncertainty of geopolitical risks and the damage posed to many sectors of the economy by higher energy costs," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "The economy was thought to have been a lost cause during much of the current Administration's time in office, but real GDP has bounced back above a 3 percent run rate in Q3 2026 for the first time in a year." Economic growth has been driven by higher levels of investment from the artificial intelligence build-out, as well as high levels of consumer and government spending. Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products. Real sales to private domestic purchasers, a proxy that Fed officials use for underlying demand, rose 4.9%, compared with a 4.6% increase in the second quarter. There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

title: Analysis: Kevin Warsh is keeping Wall Street guessing. It may be his most powerful tool
summary: The new chairman made clear he leans toward higher interest rates, but left himself options depending on how the data comes in.
body: The Federal Reserve chairman's news conference Wednesday was sharply different from his early appearances in the job, when he often seemed backed into a corner. He's shown he is willing to let the markets guess where he is going — at least to a point. And he has started using his authority to reshape the institution. Warsh was appointed by a president who said cutting interest rates was a litmus test for his choice for Fed chair. When the Federal Open Market Committee opted to hold rates flat in June and July, even with inflation well above the Fed's 2% target, a swarm of commentators questioned the new chairman's credibility. The FOMC's subsequent decision in September to raise rates came with such a hawkish reading of the economy by Warsh that the markets swung sharply in the opposite direction. Investors thought the Fed might be locked into a rate hike this week until a pair of top officials came out and appeared to deliberately temper market expectations. This week, Warsh put all that behind him. He disavowed any expectation that the Fed is on a set course: "If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he said. But Warsh also gave a strong signal that his current lean is toward higher rates. "While overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight," he said. He was preserving his options while laying the intellectual groundwork for a hike in December, should inflation remain stubborn. Warsh declined to confirm the widespread assumption in the markets that the officials who had talked down the markets had done so at his direction. Fed insiders have said that the central bank's vice chairs usually coordinate messaging with the chair. "To suggest somehow that I am some kind of all-knowing person sending messages out, that's not the committee of the FOMC that I know," Warsh said. And yet the market got the message that the Fed wouldn't hike this week. If Warsh wants to give otherwise taboo forward guidance through his lieutenants, he now has plausible deniability. This is Warsh's MO: He is intellectually flexible and highly focused on achieving his goals. For instance, one of the goals of the task forces he has assembled to kick-start policy changes is to change the way the Fed measures inflation. But that was impossible while his commitment to fighting it was in question. September's rate hike does a lot to answer the skeptics who said he wasn't serious about slowing price increases, and he is willing to deliver more rate increases, if necessary. "If you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the twos, let us disabuse you of it," Warsh said Wednesday. The target is 2% flat. His remarks are a recipe for higher rates as long as the economy stays strong. Warsh and the FOMC will have a raft of new data before the next meeting, in December, to make their case. That could, alternatively, help him make the case that productivity is rising, allowing for more growth without inflation. Meanwhile, Warsh's other changes at the Fed are starting to take effect. He announced a plan Wednesday to reduce the number of times the FOMC is scheduled to vote on interest rates over the next two years. The Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, but will skip a vote on whether to change rates at one meeting in 2027 and two in 2028. That move has the effect of devaluing a good chunk of Fedspeak. The market won't pay much mind to a marginal regional Fed president's comments when they come as much as three months ahead of a rate decision. Regional presidents also get one fewer scheduled vote in their yearlong rotations as decision-makers on the FOMC. The Fed chairman retains the authority to call an impromptu meeting at any time should he see the need to change rates. title: Here are five key takeaways from the Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference
summary: Even though the interest-rate vote went as expected, there were a few surprises out of this week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
body: The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady . At the press conference that followed, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh disclosed some of his thinking about where the U.S. economy stands, and how that affects monetary policy. But for Fed wonks, the big news may have been Warsh's disclosure of some procedural changes ahead. "The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments." —Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management. "The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." — Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist, Jefferies .

According to a report from Investing.com, the bank’s strategists led by Lina Thomas cited the hawkish shift in the Federal Reserve’s stance in recent months and its effect on investor positioning for the move. "We retain our longer-term constructive view on structurally strong central bank demand – which drives most of the 15% price upside we forecast by end-2027," the strategists said, as per the report. Goldman expects further price support once the Fed starts cutting rates in the second half of 2027, adding that higher oil prices could add further pressure through systematic selling. The quick response: enterprise and hyperscale customers are upgrading their network gear sooner than planned, and many of those investments are directly associated with the build-out of AI data centers. The technology company's stock has climbed by approximately 45% since March 31 through the early part of July 2026; the bulk of the gains have been driven by a single earnings report in May. body: Broadcom Inc.’s AI chip business is showing little sign of slowing down, with the semiconductor giant expecting revenue from its AI chips to double in each of the next two years as demand from customers including Anthropic and OpenAI accelerates. The Palo Alto, California-based company expects AI semiconductor revenue to reach about $115 billion in fiscal 2027, up from roughly $58 billion expected in 2026, CEO Hock Tan said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. The company sees another doubling to $230 billion in fiscal 2028, underscoring the strength of its custom AI accelerator and networking chip business. “In 2027, we have secured the supply to again double AI revenue to approximately $115 billion. Our demand actually exceeds this outlook, and we will work to improve supply,” Tan said. “In 2028… we have line of sight for fiscal 2028 AI semiconductor revenue growth to again double to $230 billion. Here again, we have secured the supply to meet this outlook.” Despite the strong outlook, Broadcom’s fourth-quarter revenue forecast , which implies 93% growth, came in below Wall Street’s expectations, sending AVGO shares 1.3% lower in overnight trading late Wednesday. The comments highlight how Broadcom has emerged as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom beyond Nvidia. Its custom accelerators, or XPUs, are increasingly being adopted by major AI companies looking to build their own chips. AI chip sales more than tripled to $16.7 billion in the third quarter, lifting Broadcom's total revenue 86% to $29.59 billion, beating estimates of $29.36 billion. Adjusted profit came in at $3.32 ​per share, compared with estimates of $3.24. Anthropic is expected to become Broadcom’s largest XPU customer next year, with the AI startup planning to deploy another 5 gigawatts of Broadcom-designed TPU v8i chips in 2027 and an additional 10 gigawatts in 2028. OpenAI is also expected to become a major customer, with Broadcom seeing a path for the ChatGPT maker to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of its next-generation Jalapeno XPU in 2028. “These two guys, Anthropic and OpenAI, I mean, these are… it’s like you have two geniuses in the middle of outer Mongolia. They need to go to college to fulfill their potential,” Tan said, suggesting that while both companies have enormous potential, they need access to Broadcom’s chips and infrastructure (“college”) to fully realize it. “We do what we can to help them, and part of it is creating sources of financing to help these companies with the leading-edge frontier models in the world be able to play in the same playing field and be able to offer these great technology products to the world,” he added. Broadcom has secured supplies for wafers, substrates and memory needed to meet its 2027 and 2028 AI revenue targets. The company also plans to begin deploying its Singapore substrate facility in fiscal 2027 to ease a key supply bottleneck. Moor Insights & Strategy CEO and analyst Patrick Moorhead said Broadcom delivered a “strong, but not flawless” third quarter, arguing that the key takeaway was its AI execution rather than the modest revenue beat. He pointed to Broadcom’s $16.7 billion in Q3 AI revenue and $21.7 billion Q4 outlook as evidence that the company is successfully converting its AI backlog into sales. body: AMD has a huge opportunity in the next three years stemming from inference and agentic AI. Meanwhile, the strong Democratic showing in the midterm elections put the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out on notice. Despite the political shift, I wouldn't expect there to be a major impact on overall AI infrastructure growth in the coming years, with hyperscalers being able to navigate the current environment and shifting some projects overseas. However, between AMD and Intel, I think the clear winner is likely to be AMD. Here's why. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Advanced Micro Devices has been one of the hardest-hit stocks in the semiconductor pullback. However, the company is riding two powerful waves in inference and agentic AI that are just starting to kick in, and its new Helios rack solution could be a game changer. Helios is AMD's turnkey AI infrastructure solution that incorporates its graphics processing units (GPUs), central processing units (CPUs), and networking components into a single system. The system contains 72 GPUs and 18 CPUs per rack and is designed to provide the "lowest cost per token" to help reduce overall computing costs. The system has already started being rolled out to key customers, including OpenAI, Meta Platforms , Microsoft , Anthropic, and Oracle , and OEM (original equipment manufacturer) and ODM (original design manufacturer) partners will also soon begin to ship Helios. AMD has two large deals in place with OpenAI and Meta Platforms for 6 gigawatts of compute capacity each. With each Helios system costing between $5 million and $5.5 million and consuming between 225 kilowatts and 245 kilowatts of power, each deal would be worth approximately $120 billion. Meanwhile, Anthropic's 2-gigawatt deal would be worth around $40 billion, with Microsoft and Oracle as smaller customers. At the same time, the company is seeing huge demand for its server CPUs, given that these chips are needed to help manage AI agents. Its CPUs are helping run Meta's new Muse AI agents, and the company sees server CPUs becoming a $220 billion market by 2030. As a result, AMD is projecting growth to soar next year, with it recently forecasting revenue to surge 80% in 2027. The pullback has dropped the stock to a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of around 9 times its 2030 analyst estimates, giving it plenty of room to run the next three years. While AMD has been the victim of a broader semiconductor stock sell-off, much of Intel's wounds are self-inflicted. This is due to the company's still-outsized exposure to the PC market, which is seeing weak demand as high memory costs have caused computer makers to raise prices, slowing demand. Intel's client computing and physical AI group (CCPG) remains its largest segment, and revenue for the unit fell 5% last quarter. However, the company is expecting units to drop 10% in 2027 after a 12% decline this year, which will also lead to a large inventory correction that will significantly impact the next two quarters. Meanwhile, Intel's foundry business continues to produce large losses, including a $1.9 billion operating loss in Q3.
